# Hydraulic lime, Roman concrete and Portland cement (`hydraulic_cement`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: needs lime_burning; helped by fired_brick_ceramics, coke_iron
- Core idea: Lime mortar that contains reactive silica and alumina hardens by reaction with water, even under water. Vitruvius specifies two parts volcanic ash (pozzolana) to one of lime for harbour work. His three-to-one ratio for ordinary mortar refers to pit sand; finely crushed brick or tile serves where there is no volcano. The same effect comes from burning limestone that naturally contains clay. Portland cement is made by grinding limestone and clay together (about four to one), burning the mix until it begins to fuse at about 1450 °C, and grinding the clinker fine with a few per cent of gypsum. Concrete is cement, sand and gravel at about 1:2:4 with as little water as will work, kept damp for a week.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying it 'dries'; it sets by taking up water and is ruined if it dries out or freezes while young.
  - Too much water makes weak, porous concrete.
  - Any grey powder will not do: ordinary sand or ash is inert, and the pozzolan must be tested with lime under water.
  - Burning at lime-kiln heat gives only weak hydraulic lime; true cement needs near-white heat and hard grinding.
  - The myth that the Roman recipe was lost and is stronger than modern concrete; it is durable but much weaker and slower.
- History: greece: c. 500–300 BC – lime with volcanic earth from Thera or crushed tile in cisterns (Kameiros, Rhodes); rome: c. 200 BC – pozzolana concrete in Campania; c. 20 BC Vitruvius and the harbour of Caesarea; c. AD 126 the Pantheon dome; india: ancient to Mughal – lime with brick dust (surkhi) for tanks and waterworks; islamic: medieval – lime with ash and crushed brick (sarooj) for cisterns, baths and bridges in Iran; europe: 1756–1759 Smeaton finds that clayey limestone gives hydraulic lime (Eddystone); 1796 Parker's 'Roman cement'; 1818 Vicat's artificial hydraulic lime; 1824 Aspdin's Portland cement patent; c. 1845 Isaac Johnson burns it to clinker, the modern product
- Read:
  - Vitruvius, De architectura II.6 and V.12
  - John Smeaton, A Narrative of the Building and a Description of the Construction of the Edystone Lighthouse with Stone (1791)
  - Marie D. Jackson et al., Phillipsite and Al-tobermorite mineral cements produced through low-temperature water-rock reactions in Roman marine concrete, American Mineralogist 102 (2017)
